Conditional cross-chain asset representation: May 2023 models
Research date: 29 September 2026. This study asks what the historical contract models permit under
explicit assumptions. It does not require a presently available pARB RPC, assert that a source chain is
operating, or submit transactions. Historical PulseChain observations remain separate evidence.
Principal conclusion
A source-native transferable token or vault receipt can remain locked on its origin network while an
authorized representation is minted on a destination network. Destination underlying escrow is not a
universal requirement. Historical Arbitrum reverse gateways and Omnibridge reverse-mode code provide
concrete examples; Polygon's mintable-token predicate provides a related child-burn / root-mint model.
These are distinct from ordinary return withdrawals that release pre-existing destination escrow.
This establishes a technically plausible building block for the thesis. It does not establish that the
resulting representation equals an already existing destination aT oken, OUSD, mUSD, eUSD or FRAX
token. That identity and its issuance permission are separate contract properties. A destination pool
must accept the actual token address received, and have the assets necessary for the contemplated
output.
Historical source boundary
Sources were selected at or before 10 May 2023, 22:36:11 UTC, the inherited Ethereum snapshot
boundary. A repository revision before this date demonstrates availability of that code, not universal
deployment of every feature. The Arbitrum/Optimism historical study (Appendix 13) adds direct
inherited-block reads for ARB's existing reverse integration. Current documentation is used only for
terminology or address discovery; later Across intents versions, Optimism Bedrock, Gnosis USDS/
transmuter changes, and later asset deployments are not retroactively inserted into the baseline.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 60

Across V2: liquidity delivery, not a universal token minter
The pre-cutoff source revision is a231a21df4ee58378d3f0fc8148daf5bc4791e3c, 5 May 2023. Its SpokePool accepts
deposits on enabled routes and transfers the origin token into the spoke. Normal fast fills transfer
destination tokens supplied by the relayer; supported slow-fill/refund flows use available protocol
inventory. Hub/spoke accounting and optimistic bundle validation coordinate repayment and
rebalancing. This lets funds become available before canonical settlement, but still requires destination
capital.
The historical SpokePool uses destination-token transfers for fills. The HubPool mints its own LP shares
when liquidity providers deposit L1 underlying. Those LP shares are not newly issued USDC, DAI, OUSD
or Aave aT okens.
The Arbitrum SpokePool uses a mapped token counterpart and the Arbitrum gateway router for funds
returned to the HubPool. Thus Across can be a transport/liquidity component of a broader system, but
does not eliminate the underlying bridge's token rules. Controlling a settlement component does not
cause an unrelated token contract to acquire a mint method or create absent destination cash.
Replenishment on both chains and deposits remaining on L2
Yes: Across V2's historical design can replenish spoke inventory as well as L1 hub inventory. Source-chain
user deposits add tokens to that chain's SpokePool. Positive hub-to-spoke rebalance amounts deliver
tokens from the HubPool through a configured adapter. In the other direction, relayer-refund settlement
can include an amount to return through the chain-specific bridge. Ordinary L1 LP deposits also replenish
the HubPool. The source contracts show both directions; this is not an inference from modern Across
documentation.
A normal fast fill uses a relayer's destination assets. Thus the recipient can receive existing L1 tokens
while the original deposit remains in the L2 SpokePool awaiting settlement. The relayer selects a
repayment chain, subject to the supported route and valid settlement accounting. Repayment on L2 can
leave the assets on that network, but transfers them out of the spoke to the relayer. Repayment on L1
consumes L1 inventory instead. Neither operation creates an unrestricted new stablecoin balance from a
remote deposit alone.
Ignoring fees, a conceptual 100-unit example illustrates the first case:

The source user spent 100 on L2; the recipient received 100 on L1; the relayer exchanged the location of
its inventory. No canonical bridge transfer of those 100 units is necessary in this abstract case if the
supported settlement route permits the L2 refund. This is a conditional liquidity exchange, not a record
of an observed PulseChain bundle.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 61

Across's bundle structure includes net-send amounts and running balances rather than requiring every
individual deposit to move through a canonical bridge immediately. Opposing flows and local refund
needs can therefore reduce gross cross-chain rebalancing. A continuously replenished spoke may keep a
positive balance while L1 recipients continue receiving fills. A persistent pool balance does not mean the
same deposit remains exclusively reserved for its original depositor: obligations are pooled and settled
across flows.
For a one-direction stream, finite L1 relayer/protocol inventory eventually needs replacement.
Replenishing only the L2 spoke does not itself replenish L1 cash. Continued L1 delivery needs incoming
L1 funds, offsetting business, completed bridge returns or another explicitly funded arrangement. If an
ordinary canonical return is blocked by missing L1 escrow, Across's advance does not remove that
settlement problem. Local L2 refunds can change which party bears inventory exposure, but they do not
grant destination mint authority.
This is the precise sense in which a “reverse lock and release” analogy is useful: source custody can
coexist with destination payment funded elsewhere. It is not a generic permanent lock/L1-
representation-mint function. In the historical code, source deposit does not automatically mint L1 LP
shares. The HubPool's ordinary LP issuance requires an L1 underlying deposit, and receipt valuation
involving utilized reserves should not be confused with immediately spendable L1 cash.
Source anchors are the pinned HubPool's root-bundle rebalance logic, the pinned SpokePool's fill/refund
logic, and the Arbitrum spoke's canonical-return adapter, linked above. These are contract capability
statements, not claims that all corresponding copied routes, actors and balances are currently
operational.
L2 capital supporting an L1 DeFi action
Across can economically connect a source deposit to a destination DeFi action: The recipient spends the
destination tokens provided by a relayer or an inventory-funded slow fill. Compatible local calls can be
composed in one L1 transaction. The source deposit, destination execution and later settlement remain
separate transactions across chains. Local atomic execution does not make the complete cross-chain
transaction atomic.
For example, assuming a supported route and ignoring fees, a 100-unit L2 deposit can support a relayer
delivering 100 existing units on L1. A recipient integration could supply those units to Aave, receiving
aT okens, or exchange them in a Curve pool. Aave must accept that exact underlying and permit supply;
Curve must accept that exact input and have available output liquidity. The L2 deposit remains part of
the bridge's settlement obligations. These are conditional applications of ordinary funded transfers, not
evidence of a historically executed PulseChain route or a claim of profitable arbitrage.

The configured-spoke discovery corrects the earlier overextension of the older spoke's limitation. The
first deployment inspected was not the spoke selected by the sampled HubPool mapping. Source-backed
conclusions must follow the exact proxy and implementation at the specified block. See the configured-
spoke audit (Appendix 14) and the inherited implementation source.
The deployed-spoke finding uses the historical deployment artifact and explorer-published contract
source. The published contract is a directly deployed, constructor-based contract; its sampled EIP-1967
implementation slots are zero. The complete runtime is 17,282 bytes at both comparison blocks, with
SHA-256 9a42b4065ba8533d92f7de422d2fe944a609444e543dbb4bb3a4445ff4b9e4b9. This is an endpoint comparison and
source inspection, not an independent compiler reproduction or an exhaustive discovery of additional
spoke deployments.
The proposed source's callback follows the funded transfer and is not wrapped in an outer try/catch. If its
failure propagates, the destination transaction reverts, including its transfer; receiver logic could instead
handle an inner failure itself. An ordinary ERC-20 transfer in the older deployed spoke does not
automatically invoke a receiving contract's arbitrary DeFi logic. An additional authorized L1 coordinator
could compose compatible fill and receiver calls, but no such deployed integration or historical execution
is established by this study. A native callback and external transaction composition are different
integration cases.
Further inspection of the published deployed source resolves another possible shortcut: its inherited 
MultiCaller.multicall uses address(this).delegatecall for each item. It batches methods on the spoke itself; it
is not an arbitrary external-target executor for Aave or Curve. Its presence therefore does not replace a
recipient callback or the separate authorized L1 integration described above. The ordinary fillRelay is
public and is not limited to externally owned accounts, so the reviewed interface does not categorically
exclude composition by a contract. That compatibility is narrower than proof that a specific funded
coordinator exists or that an entire route has executed successfully.
Consequently, local arbitrage can be atomic if the local contracts and funding permit it; a profitable
cross-chain arbitrage round trip is not guaranteed. Any L1 flash loan must be repaid using funds
available before that L1 transaction ends. A future L2 reimbursement cannot itself repay it inside that
transaction. The research does not assume an oracle quote or a remote balance makes absent L1 tokens
available for transfer.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 63

Observed control and L1 inventory
The Across/UMA control audit (Appendix 3) establishes a HubPool ownership transfer to 0xfeca…d140 on 19
June 2026 and an Across OptimisticGovernor module ownership transfer to e121 on 19 August 2026.
These are relevant governance changes. The sampled UMA infrastructure did not show corresponding
ownership transfers, and common human ownership remains unproved. Administrative control alone
does not supply destination tokens.
At the fixed endpoint, the HubPool's actual copied DAI, USDC and USDT balances and its stored liquid
reserves are all zero. Its stored utilized reserves are respectively 1,656,490.776260091143953778 DAI,
16,210,612.259813 USDC and 500,442.221859 USDT. Utilized-reserve accounting is not immediately
spendable cash or independent proof that remote receivables are collectible. These reads do not
establish the balances of all spokes, external relayers or prospective funders, and do not rule out funded
delivery from those other sources.
Reproduction evidence is preserved in the ignored batch artifacts/parb-across-accounting-20260929/:
historical deployment artifacts, reserve_reads.json, lp_inventory.json, spoke_implementations.json, 
spoke_17232999.json, spoke_27659393.json, and spoke_source.json. State reads use the same single public RPC
and fixed endpoint as the main paper. No state-changing transactions or route simulations were
submitted.
Omnibridge: a historical reverse representation model
Pre-cutoff source revision c814f686487c50462b132b9691fd77cc2de237d3, 6 September 2021 contains reverse-
mode support in both Home and Foreign mediators. Gnosis is a separate chain, not an Ethereum rollup;
Omnibridge uses the Arbitrary Message Bridge's authentication model. The same representation analysis
can still be applied to a hypothetical copied counterpart.
The shared historical mediator logic distinguishes source-native assets from already-bridged
representations. A source-native deposit increases accounted escrow and requests a mapped
representation on the other side. A representation returning to its origin is burned, allowing origin escrow
to be released. The destination can deploy a bridge-controlled token representation when none exists.
Consequently, a token originating on the Gnosis side can conceptually be escrowed there and
represented on the Ethereum/PulseChain side without pre-existing L1 underlying escrow, where the
reverse-mode mediator configuration supports it.
The Foreign mediator retains execution-limit checks and uses the shared distinction between release and
mint. A custom existing representation must support the expected authorized mint/burn behavior.
Standard representation tokens are ERC-677-compatible, which includes ordinary ERC-20 transfer
behavior. This compatibility does not automatically map a newly created representation into an existing
Curve or Balancer pool.
Fixed-balance vault shares provide clearer escrow units than raw rebasing balances. Interest, transfer
fees, rebases, rounding and redemption restrictions still need asset-specific accounting. This study
establishes the historical model; it does not establish the exact reverse-mode activation, mapping or
issuer authority for every copied PulseChain token.
The separate xDAI bridge must not be conflated with this generic model. Its DAI-origin return path
releases DAI backing; it is not a general right to mint arbitrary destination DAI. Current Gnosis
documentation contains later changes that do not form part of this May 2023 analysis.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 64

Polygon PoS mintable assets: a distinct burn/mint example
The pre-cutoff revision ece4e54546a4e075f3a03b2699bc6bd92a5bc065, 3 April 2023 contains MintableERC20Predicate.
Its authenticated exit model processes a child-token burn and, if root-token inventory is insufficient,
invokes the root token's authorized mint before paying the withdrawal. Ordinary root-origin ERC-20
escrow predicates are a different path. Polygon PoS is also not interchangeable with an optimistic-rollup
security model.
This is another historical example where an authorized destination issuance path need not start with
enough root escrow. The root token must actually be mintable by that predicate and have the
appropriate mapping. Source burn, message/exit validation and destination issuance remain necessary
accounting links. The existence of a generic mintable predicate does not make all existing DAI or USDC
contracts mintable by it. Historical predicate source.
A conditional proposition for the thesis
Let a source protocol issue q transferable receipt shares after a valid local deposit. Assume the shares
are genuinely locked, the bridge recognizes that lock under its specified trust model, destination claims
are issued only once, and redemption extinguishes the corresponding claim before releasing those
shares. The bridge can then issue a representation backed by those source shares while the underlying
remains in the source protocol. No second L1 copy of that underlying is logically necessary for this
representation model.
If the issued destination token is the exact token accepted by a destination pool, and that pool's rules
and available balances permit output y > 0 DAI, then trading that representation for y DAI is mechanically
possible. The counterparty/pool receives the remote-backed claim and the trader receives existing DAI.
This is exchange of claims against an existing inventory; it is not proof that a new externally redeemable
dollar was created.
For an ordinary L1 Aave aT oken, Portal supplies a different accounting link: it creates the destination
reserve's aT oken while recording outstanding unbacked issuance. Until destination underlying arrives,
source escrow alone does not remove that local unbacked balance. A wrapper can hold the correct
ordinary aT oken, but wrapper compatibility does not establish completed Portal settlement. These two
accounting models should not be merged into one claim of universally fully backed L1 Aave liquidity.
This proposition supports conditional possibility, including purchases of pDAI when the stated
acceptance and liquidity conditions hold. It does not prove the required token integrations already exist,
identify an operator, or guarantee scale, profitability, permanent liquidity replenishment or a $1
external-value peg.
How the evidence strengthens the paper
The appropriate framework has three categories: historical mechanism available, observed copied
deployment or transaction, and explicit scenario assumption. A missing source RPC belongs in the third
category for source execution; it is not a reason to reject the mathematical possibility. Conversely, broad
administrator control cannot be used to quietly replace a missing mechanism with arbitrary hypothetical
code and call it an inherited capability.
The strong theoretical case specifies the receipt actually locked, the exact representation actually
minted, its existing pool acceptance, conserved share accounting, and finite output inventory. The audit
already contributes actual ARB destination minting, Aave wrapper acceptance, e121 mUSD-to-DAI
purchases, and examined-wallet repayments. These support individual links without pretending they
constitute one historically verified end-to-end transaction.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 65

Source snapshots and cutoff metadata are preserved in ignored artifacts/parb-historical-models-20260929/.
No new contract deployments, transactions, privileged simulations or transaction payloads were
produced.
Inherited-block presence reads also found code at the copied Foreign Omnibridge proxy 
0x88ad09518695c6c3712ac10a214be5109a655671, whose implementation getter returned 
0x8eb3b7d8498a6716904577b2579e1c313d48e347, and the Polygon mintable predicate proxy 
0x9923263fa127b3d1484cfd649df8f1831c2a74e4, returning 0x0f92d459b20d21f6bf9e02056ea9165d3f78ba62. The explorer
publishes ForeignOmnibridge source for the former implementation, including representation handling. It did
not return verified source for the latter implementation. These reads establish inherited L1 infrastructure
presence, not every source counterpart, asset mapping or effective permission. Records are in 
copied_bridge_presence.json and the implementation-source responses.

Omnibridge: a historical reverse representation model
Pre-cutoff source revision c814f686487c50462b132b9691fd77cc2de237d3, 6 September 2021 contains reverse-
mode support in both Home and Foreign mediators. Gnosis is a separate chain, not an Ethereum rollup;
Omnibridge uses the Arbitrary Message Bridge's authentication model. The same representation analysis
can still be applied to a hypothetical copied counterpart.
The shared historical mediator logic distinguishes source-native assets from already-bridged
representations. A source-native deposit increases accounted escrow and requests a mapped
representation on the other side. A representation returning to its origin is burned, allowing origin escrow
to be released. The destination can deploy a bridge-controlled token representation when none exists.
Consequently, a token originating on the Gnosis side can conceptually be escrowed there and
represented on the Ethereum/PulseChain side without pre-existing L1 underlying escrow, where the
reverse-mode mediator configuration supports it.
The Foreign mediator retains execution-limit checks and uses the shared distinction between release and
mint. A custom existing representation must support the expected authorized mint/burn behavior.
Standard representation tokens are ERC-677-compatible, which includes ordinary ERC-20 transfer
behavior. This compatibility does not automatically map a newly created representation into an existing
Curve or Balancer pool.
Fixed-balance vault shares provide clearer escrow units than raw rebasing balances. Interest, transfer
fees, rebases, rounding and redemption restrictions still need asset-specific accounting. This study
establishes the historical model; it does not establish the exact reverse-mode activation, mapping or
issuer authority for every copied PulseChain token.
The separate xDAI bridge must not be conflated with this generic model. Its DAI-origin return path
releases DAI backing; it is not a general right to mint arbitrary destination DAI. Current Gnosis
documentation contains later changes that do not form part of this May 2023 analysis.

A conditional proposition for the thesis
Let a source protocol issue q transferable receipt shares after a valid local deposit. Assume the shares
are genuinely locked, the bridge recognizes that lock under its specified trust model, destination claims
are issued only once, and redemption extinguishes the corresponding claim before releasing those
shares. The bridge can then issue a representation backed by those source shares while the underlying
remains in the source protocol. No second L1 copy of that underlying is logically necessary for this
representation model.
If the issued destination token is the exact token accepted by a destination pool, and that pool's rules
and available balances permit output y > 0 DAI, then trading that representation for y DAI is mechanically
possible. The counterparty/pool receives the remote-backed claim and the trader receives existing DAI.
This is exchange of claims against an existing inventory; it is not proof that a new externally redeemable
dollar was created.
For an ordinary L1 Aave aT oken, Portal supplies a different accounting link: it creates the destination
reserve's aT oken while recording outstanding unbacked issuance. Until destination underlying arrives,
source escrow alone does not remove that local unbacked balance. A wrapper can hold the correct
ordinary aT oken, but wrapper compatibility does not establish completed Portal settlement. These two
accounting models should not be merged into one claim of universally fully backed L1 Aave liquidity.
This proposition supports conditional possibility, including purchases of pDAI when the stated
acceptance and liquidity conditions hold. It does not prove the required token integrations already exist,
identify an operator, or guarantee scale, profitability, permanent liquidity replenishment or a $1
external-value peg.
How the evidence strengthens the paper
The appropriate framework has three categories: historical mechanism available, observed copied
deployment or transaction, and explicit scenario assumption. A missing source RPC belongs in the third
category for source execution; it is not a reason to reject the mathematical possibility. Conversely, broad
administrator control cannot be used to quietly replace a missing mechanism with arbitrary hypothetical
code and call it an inherited capability.
The strong theoretical case specifies the receipt actually locked, the exact representation actually
minted, its existing pool acceptance, conserved share accounting, and finite output inventory. The audit
already contributes actual ARB destination minting, Aave wrapper acceptance, e121 mUSD-to-DAI
purchases, and examined-wallet repayments. These support individual links without pretending they
constitute one historically verified end-to-end transaction.
